findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Saudi Arabia
findings.description:
Kafala system and domestic worker exclusions from labor law protections

Scheme: Recruitment agencies and employers confiscate migrant workers' passports upon arrival, enforce excessive working hours (often 18+ hours/day), and withhold wages under threat of deportation or false accusations. Workers are excluded from the Saudi Labor Law (Royal Decree No. M/51, 2005) if they are domestic workers, leaving them with no legal recourse for wage theft, physical abuse, or contract violations. Employers exploit the 'sponsorship transfer' restriction to prevent workers from changing jobs, effectively trapping them in forced labor conditions.
tags: Saudi Labor Law (Royal Decree No. M/51, 2005) - Article 7 (exclusion of domestic workers)
Kafala (Sponsorship) System - Ministerial Resolution No. 1676 (2015)
Anti-Trafficking Law (Royal Decree No. M/40, 2009) - rarely enforced for labor exploitation cases
SA

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Qatar
findings.description:
Partial Kafala reforms with persistent Wage Protection System (WPS) gaps and recruitment fee loopholes

Scheme: Employers exploit the 'no-objection certificate' (NOC) requirement for job changes, which was nominally abolished in 2020 but is still informally enforced. Recruitment agencies charge migrant workers illegal fees (up to $3,000 USD) for jobs, trapping them in debt bondage. The WPS, designed to ensure timely wage payments, is bypassed by employers who pay workers partially in cash or delay payments until the end of contracts. Workers in the construction sector (e.g., FIFA World Cup projects) are particularly vulnerable, as subcontractors exploit the lack of enforcement of Law No. 17 of 2020 (on wage protection).
tags: Law No. 17 of 2020 (Wage Protection System) - Article 3 (non-compliance penalties rarely enforced)
Law No. 21 of 2015 (Reformed Kafala System) - Article 21 (NOC requirement abolished but informally enforced)
Ministerial Decision No. 21 of 2019 (on recruitment fees) - unenforced for agencies operating in sending countries
QA

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Thailand
findings.description:
Fishing vessel exemptions from labor law and border worker registration gaps

Scheme: Broker networks traffic migrant workers (primarily from Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos) into Thailand’s fishing industry using fraudulent documents or no documents at all. The Fisheries Act (B.E. 2558, 2015) and Labor Protection Act (B.E. 2541, 1998) exempt fishing vessels from key labor protections, including maximum working hours and minimum wage requirements. Workers are forced to work 20+ hour shifts, paid below minimum wage, and confined to boats for months or years. Employers exploit the lack of registration for border workers (under the Royal Ordinance on Foreign Workers Management B.E. 2560, 2017) to avoid oversight and threaten workers with deportation if they complain.
tags: Fisheries Act (B.E. 2558, 2015) - Section 5 (exemption for fishing vessels)
Labor Protection Act (B.E. 2541, 1998) - Section 4 (exclusion of fishing sector)
Royal Ordinance on Foreign Workers Management (B.E. 2560, 2017) - Section 13 (registration gaps for border workers)
TH

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Malaysia
findings.description:
Labor outsourcing companies and sectoral exemptions in plantations and electronics manufacturing

Scheme: Labor outsourcing companies (e.g., in the electronics and plantation sectors) recruit migrant workers (primarily from Bangladesh, Nepal, and Indonesia) and lease them to employers under short-term contracts. These companies exploit the Employment Act 1955 (amended 2022), which allows for 'contract labor' without providing workers the same protections as direct employees. Workers are charged exorbitant recruitment fees (up to $5,000 USD), leading to debt bondage. In the plantation sector, employers use the 'piece-rate' payment system to avoid minimum wage requirements. The Electronics Industry Code of Conduct (EICC) is voluntary and rarely enforced, enabling forced overtime and wage theft in factories supplying global brands.
tags: Employment Act 1955 (amended 2022) - Section 2 (definition of 'contract labor' excludes protections)
Minimum Wages Order 2022 - exemptions for piece-rate workers in agriculture
Anti-Trafficking in Persons and Anti-Smuggling of Migrants Act 2007 - rarely enforced for labor exploitation
MY

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Lebanon
findings.description:
Strict Kafala system with no labor law coverage for domestic workers and normalized confiscation of documents

Scheme: Recruitment agencies and employers in Lebanon exploit the Kafala system to trap migrant domestic workers (primarily from Ethiopia, the Philippines, and Bangladesh) in conditions of forced labor. The Lebanese Labor Law (Decree No. 32/1, 1946) explicitly excludes domestic workers, leaving them with no legal protections for working hours, wages, or abuse. Employers routinely confiscate passports, enforce 24/7 work schedules, and withhold wages under threat of deportation. The Standard Unified Contract for Domestic Workers (2020) is rarely enforced, and workers who escape are criminalized for 'absconding' under General Security regulations. The economic crisis has exacerbated exploitation, with employers paying wages in devalued Lebanese pounds or not at all.
tags: Lebanese Labor Law (Decree No. 32/1, 1946) - Article 7 (exclusion of domestic workers)
Standard Unified Contract for Domestic Workers (2020) - unenforced
General Security Regulations - criminalization of 'absconding' workers
LB

findings.title: Cross-jurisdiction pattern: labor_law_gaps
findings.description: Criminals exploit migration corridors by combining jurisdiction-specific gaps to create 'exploitation chains.' For example: (1) Recruitment agencies in sending countries (e.g., Nepal, Bangladesh) charge illegal fees, trapping workers in debt bondage before they even depart. (2) Employers in destination jurisdictions (e.g., Saudi Arabia, Lebanon) exploit Kafala systems to confiscate passports and restrict movement. (3) Labor outsourcing companies in Malaysia or Thailand use contract labor loopholes to avoid providing benefits, while subcontractors in Qatar or Saudi Arabia bypass wage protection systems. (4) Traffickers move workers between jurisdictions (e.g., Thailand to Malaysia) to reset legal protections and avoid detection. These chains rely on asymmetries in labor laws, enforcement gaps, and the criminalization of undocumented workers, making it nearly impossible for victims to seek recourse.
tags: cross_jurisdiction
meta_pattern

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: DeFi (No Jurisdiction)
findings.description:
Regulatory void - absence of KYC/AML requirements, pseudonymous transactions, and smart contract automation enabling irreversible, cross-border transfers without oversight.

Scheme: Criminals exploit DeFi protocols to launder money through 'mixing' services (e.g., Tornado Cash) or cross-chain bridges to obfuscate transaction trails. Funds are moved from illicit sources (e.g., ransomware, darknet markets) into DeFi liquidity pools, swapped across multiple tokens, and withdrawn as 'clean' assets. Smart contracts automate this process, making it difficult for authorities to trace or seize funds.
tags: No direct laws (jurisdictionless), but may violate:
1. FATF Travel Rule (Recommendation 16) - requires VASPs to share originator/beneficiary info for transactions >$1,000.
2. U.S. Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) - applies to 'money transmitters' but DeFi protocols argue they are not financial institutions.
3. EU's 6AMLD - criminalizes enabling money laundering, but enforcement is challenging without a legal entity to target.
GLOBAL

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: El Salvador
findings.description:
Bitcoin as legal tender with minimal crypto-specific regulation, residency-by-investment program, and lack of robust AML enforcement for crypto transactions.

Scheme: Criminals exploit El Salvador's Bitcoin Law (Decree No. 57) to establish shell companies or obtain residency via Bitcoin investments. They then use local Bitcoin ATMs or peer-to-peer (P2P) exchanges to convert illicit fiat into Bitcoin, leveraging the lack of KYC requirements for small transactions. Funds are moved to offshore entities or mixed via DeFi protocols. The residency program provides a veneer of legitimacy for tax evasion or sanctions evasion.
tags: 1. Bitcoin Law (Decree No. 57) - makes Bitcoin legal tender but does not impose AML/KYC requirements on individuals or businesses.
2. Ley de Lavado de Dinero y Activos (Money Laundering Law) - applies to financial institutions but not explicitly to crypto exchanges or P2P platforms.
3. Residency-by-Investment Program - requires $100K+ in Bitcoin or real estate investment but has weak vetting for source of funds.
SV

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: UAE (VASP Hub)
findings.description:
Light-touch VASP licensing in free zones (e.g., DMCC, ADGM), privacy-friendly corporate structures, and lack of public beneficial ownership registries. Exchanges in free zones operate under local regulations that are less stringent than FATF standards.

Scheme: Criminals establish Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs) in UAE free zones (e.g., DMCC Crypto Centre) to obtain a veneer of legitimacy. They exploit weak KYC/AML controls to onboard high-risk clients (e.g., sanctioned individuals, darknet market operators) and facilitate large-scale crypto-to-fiat conversions. Free zone entities can also issue privacy-friendly corporate structures (e.g., RAK ICC) to obscure beneficial ownership. Funds are then moved to offshore accounts or reinvested in real estate.
tags: 1. UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering - applies to financial institutions but enforcement is inconsistent in free zones.
2. DMCC Crypto Centre Regulations - require VASP licensing but allow for 'light' KYC for certain clients.
3. ADGM Regulatory Framework for Virtual Assets - follows FATF standards but lacks transparency in enforcement actions.
4. RAK ICC Business Companies Regulations - allow for nominee directors and shareholders, obscuring beneficial ownership.
AE

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Malta
findings.description:
Early crypto framework with exchange licensing but weak enforcement, lack of clarity on DeFi regulation, and delays in implementing EU's 5AMLD/6AMLD. The Malta Financial Services Authority (MFSA) has been criticized for rubber-stamping VASP licenses without rigorous oversight.

Scheme: Criminals obtain VASP licenses in Malta to gain access to EU banking channels, then exploit weak ongoing compliance monitoring to facilitate illicit transactions. For example, a licensed exchange may onboard high-risk clients (e.g., darknet market vendors) and fail to report suspicious transactions. Funds are moved to non-compliant DeFi protocols or mixed via privacy coins. Malta's delayed implementation of 6AMLD also allows for gaps in criminal liability for enabling money laundering.
tags: 1. Virtual Financial Assets Act (VFAA) - regulates VASPs but has been criticized for weak enforcement.
2. Malta Financial Services Authority (MFSA) Rulebook - outlines AML/CFT requirements but lacks teeth in practice.
3. EU 5AMLD/6AMLD - Malta has been slow to transpose these directives, creating temporary regulatory gaps.
4. Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) - criminalizes money laundering but prosecutions are rare for crypto-related cases.
MT

findings.title: Cross-jurisdiction pattern: crypto_regulation_gaps
findings.description: Criminals exploit regulatory asymmetries by combining jurisdictions in a 'chain of obfuscation.' For example: 1) Convert illicit fiat to Bitcoin in El Salvador using P2P exchanges to avoid KYC; 2) Move Bitcoin to a UAE-licensed VASP in a free zone to gain a veneer of legitimacy; 3) Use the VASP to swap Bitcoin for privacy coins (e.g., Monero) or move funds to a DeFi protocol; 4) Cash out via a Maltese VASP with weak compliance monitoring or a non-compliant exchange. This multi-jurisdictional approach leverages the strengths of each jurisdiction (e.g., El Salvador's lack of KYC, UAE's free zones, Malta's EU access) while mitigating risks (e.g., avoiding jurisdictions with strong enforcement like the U.S. or Singapore).
tags: cross_jurisdiction
meta_pattern

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Jebel Ali Free Zone (United Arab Emirates)
findings.description:
Minimal customs oversight and lack of stringent due diligence on gold trading and re-export transactions. The UAE Federal Decree-Law No. (20) of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering (AML) exempts free zones from certain reporting requirements, particularly for high-value commodities like gold.

Scheme: Criminals exploit JAFZA's gold trading hub status by importing gold from conflict zones (e.g., Africa) under falsified documentation, claiming it as 'recycled' or 'ethically sourced.' The gold is then re-exported to refineries in Switzerland or India with inflated invoices to justify illicit funds. The lack of end-use verification allows for trade-based money laundering (TBML), where the value of the gold is manipulated to move and clean dirty money.
tags: UAE Federal Decree-Law No. (20) of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT)
Jebel Ali Free Zone Authority (JAFZA) Regulations, Article 12 (Customs and Trade Facilitation)
UAE Cabinet Decision No. (10) of 2019 on the Executive Regulations of Federal Decree-Law No. (20) of 2018 (exemptions for free zones)
AE-JAFZA

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: Colon Free Zone (Panama)
findings.description:
Lack of end-user verification for goods transiting through the zone, combined with weak enforcement of trade documentation requirements. Panama's Law 41 of 2004 (Free Zone Law) does not mandate disclosure of beneficial ownership for companies operating in the CFZ, and the zone is exempt from Panama's stricter AML laws under Decree No. 520 of 2005.

Scheme: Criminals establish shell companies in the CFZ to facilitate trade-based money laundering through re-invoicing. For example, a company imports electronics from China at $100 per unit but invoices the buyer in Colombia at $150 per unit. The $50 difference per unit is deposited into offshore accounts as 'legitimate' profits. The lack of end-user verification allows criminals to obscure the true nature of the trade and launder proceeds from drug trafficking or corruption.
tags: Panama Law 41 of 2004 (Free Zone Law)
Panama Decree No. 520 of 2005 (AML exemptions for free zones)
Panama Law 23 of 2015 (AML/CFT, which does not fully apply to CFZ)
PA-CFZ

findings.title: Jurisdiction gap: China Free Trade Zones (e.g., Shanghai, Guangdong)
findings.description:
Loopholes in cross-border RMB flows and capital account convertibility. China's Regulations on Foreign Exchange Administration (2008) and the People's Bank of China (PBOC) Notice on Cross-Border RMB Business (2012) allow FTZs to bypass certain capital controls, but lack robust monitoring of trade misinvoicing. The FTZs also operate under separate customs regulations (e.g., Shanghai FTZ Customs Regulations, 2013), which do not require detailed end-use verification for re-exports.

Scheme: Criminals exploit the FTZs' cross-border RMB facilitation to conduct trade misinvoicing. For example, a Chinese company in the Shanghai FTZ imports machinery from Germany at $1 million but invoices it at $1.5 million. The $500,000 difference is deposited into an offshore account as 'legitimate' RMB profits. The funds are then converted to foreign currency and moved to tax havens. The lack of oversight on re-export documentation allows criminals to obscure the true value of goods and launder proceeds from corruption or tax evasion.
tags: China Regulations on Foreign Exchange Administration (2008)
PBOC Notice on Cross-Border RMB Business (2012)
Shanghai FTZ Customs Regulations (2013)
China Anti-Money Laundering Law (2006, amended 2020, with limited FTZ enforcement)
CN-FTZ

findings.title: Cross-jurisdiction pattern: free_trade_zones
findings.description: Criminals combine these free trade zones in a 'trade laundering chain' to maximize opacity. For example: 1) Gold is sourced from conflict zones and imported into Jebel Ali Free Zone (AE-JAFZA) with falsified documentation. 2) The gold is re-exported to a company in the Colon Free Zone (PA-CFZ), where re-invoicing inflates its value. 3) The overvalued gold is then shipped to a China Free Trade Zone (CN-FTZ), where cross-border RMB flows are exploited to convert the illicit proceeds into 'legitimate' trade profits. 4) The funds are finally transferred to offshore accounts in tax havens like the British Virgin Islands or Panama. Each jurisdiction's regulatory gaps (minimal customs oversight, lack of end-user verification, and capital flow loopholes) are exploited sequentially to obscure the origin, ownership, and movement of illicit funds.
tags: cross_jurisdiction
